facts.claim: "H.B.W" was released on 21 November 2024 as a single through Dirty Hit, ahead of Saya Gray's debut album SAYA (21 February 2025).
The YouTube/Virgin Music Group credits list Saya Gray as composer and writer of "H.B.W", and the track is ℗ 2024 Dirty Hit.
The album version of the track, listed as "H.B.W." on the LIE DOWN.. release, credits Saya Gray as mixing engineer, composer, writer and producer.
"H.B.W" is an acronym of the chorus lyric 'Heartbreak Wake'. Gray described it only as "the pain of nightmares".
Press materials describe the song as a fever-dream pop/avant-garde track with quiet vocals over a deep, trembling bassline. They say its lyrics confront grief and loss of control.
It follows the country-tinged single "SHELL ( OF A MAN )" and is track 8 of the 10-track album SAYA.
Gray began SAYA after a troubled romance ended. She booked a flight to Japan in autumn 2023 and took a solo cross-country road trip with an acoustic guitar.
A Paper-sourced review calls "H.B.W" an outlier on SAYA because of its trap beats and droning bass.
SAYA was co-produced by Gray and her brother Lucian, who played Buchla synthesiser and guitars. L. Young mixed it.

Gray was born in Toronto to a Japanese mother and a Scottish-Canadian father. She started out in a Jamaican Pentecostal church house band and later toured as bassist and musical director for Daniel Caesar and Willow Smith.

research.lineage: Gray's work blends art-pop, R&B, folk and field recordings, and SAYA drew on Beatles/Led Zeppelin album-making and Canadian folk forebear Joni Mitchell, while "H.B.W" itself leans toward trap-influenced avant-pop.

draft:
One time through the refrain of **H.B.W**, the line breaks off on the first letter of "heartbreak," as if the singer got jolted awake before the word could land. It's a small cut, and it tells you what kind of song this is. Saya Gray has said the title, an acronym for "Heartbreak Wake," is about "the pain of nightmares," and the phrase works both ways: the morning after a bad dream, and a vigil for something dead.

The dead thing is a relationship, and the narrator keeps visiting it. "I lay a flower once a week for you and me" is the line that hurts most. The mourner sounds devoted rather than angry, still tending a grave dug for two. Earlier, the narrator describes being treated as disposable: "I'm an outfit you change into." That's someone who understands they were worn, then dropped. The chorus doesn't fight back. It shrugs at a life that keeps flying overhead and decides that resisting is pointless. Press around the single framed it as grief and loss of control, and that tracks. But the sharpest moment is less settled than either. The narrator asks whether he's lonelier than last year, then adds, "I don't know if anybody can love you like me." It's tender and a little proud, maybe even hoping he's suffering. The song lets those feelings sit together, and they never resolve.

The sound keeps all of this close. A clean electric guitar picks out an arpeggio through a slight delay. A bass holds simple, sustained notes underneath. A drum machine ticks at a swung mid-tempo with a prominent snare and hi-hat. Gray's voice is breathy and somewhat high, singing long melodic lines with no harmonies to cushion them. It's recorded dry and close, with a raw edge, so it feels less like a performance and more like someone talking themselves down at 4 a.m.

Gray wrote it and, on the album version, is credited as producer and mixing engineer. It arrived after the country-leaning "SHELL ( OF A MAN )" and sits eighth on her debut, SAYA, a record she began after a troubled romance ended, with a trip to Japan and a solo road trip carrying an acoustic guitar. SAYA nods to Joni Mitchell's confessional plainness. **H.B.W** carries that candor into trap-influenced avant-pop, and one review singled it out as the album's outlier. The lyric ends on the title phrase, repeated, with nothing left to add.

The song holds you inside someone who knows the love is over and still brings flowers, and it makes that loyalty feel like both the wound and the only comfort.
